title: He Built a Credit-Card App With $1 Million of His Own Money. Now He Runs WhatsApp for 3 Billion People.
excerpt: Meta tapped CRED founder Kunal Shah to lead its biggest messaging platform, invested $900 million in his startup, and handed an Indian entrepreneur the keys to one of the world's most-used products.
body:
When Meta's chief product officer Chris Cox began calling entrepreneurs across India, Brazil and Mexico earlier this year, he was looking for advice. He wanted to understand how WhatsApp — a product used by more than three billion people — should evolve in the countries where it matters most.

One of those calls was with Kunal Shah. It was supposed to be a consultation. It became a job interview.

"He had an incredible set of answers," Cox told Bloomberg. By the end of the conversation, Meta's leadership was no longer asking Shah for ideas about WhatsApp's next leader. They were asking whether he wanted the job himself.

Three months of meetings in California followed, including sessions with CEO Mark Zuckerberg. On Monday, Meta announced that Shah — a 47-year-old Indian founder with no engineering degree and no Silicon Valley pedigree — would succeed Will Cathcart as WhatsApp's global head. Cathcart, who oversaw the platform's growth from 1.5 billion to more than 3 billion users over nearly seven years, will move into a new internal role focused on AI-driven consumer products.

## The Builder From Mumbai

Shah's path to WhatsApp's corner office began in India's first wave of digital payments. He co-founded FreeCharge, a mobile recharge platform that Snapdeal acquired for roughly $450 million. After exiting between 2015 and 2018, he spent time investing — backing more than 250 startups, including Razorpay and Gojek — before putting $1 million of his own capital into a new venture.


![Mark Zuckerberg — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0e/F20250904AH-2824_%2854778373111%29_%283x4_cropped_on_Zuckerberg_following_the_rule_of_thirds%29.jpg)



> **""He had an incredible set of answers," Cox told Bloomberg."**



That venture was CRED, a Bengaluru-based fintech that started by rewarding people for paying their credit card bills on time. The concept sounded modest. The execution was not. Between 2019 and 2025, CRED grew from zero to 17 million members, raised more than $900 million from global investors, secured a full stack of regulatory licences, and scaled its annual revenue to roughly $325 million across payments, lending, insurance, wealth management and commerce. In 2026, it posted its first profitable quarter.

## The $900 Million Bet

Shah's appointment did not come alone. Meta simultaneously invested $900 million in CRED through a combination of primary and secondary share purchases, valuing the startup at approximately $4.5 billion and making Meta a minority investor with about a 20 per cent stake.

"Kunal built CRED into one of India's most important technology companies, and he brings the kind of builder mentality and global perspective that will serve him well in running the world's biggest messaging app," Zuckerberg said in a statement.

Shah clarified that Meta would have no access to CRED's member data. He will retain his personal shareholding in the company while stepping back from day-to-day operations. Miten Sampat, who has led strategy and finance at CRED since 2020, will serve as interim CEO.

## Why India Matters to WhatsApp's Future


![Silicon Valley — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Silicon_Valley%2C_facing_southward_towards_Downtown_San_Jose%2C_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg/3840px-Silicon_Valley%2C_facing_southward_towards_Downtown_San_Jose%2C_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg)


India is WhatsApp's largest market — home to more than 500 million of the platform's 3.3 billion monthly active users. But for all its reach, WhatsApp has struggled to monetise. WhatsApp Pay gained traction in India's booming UPI ecosystem, yet it remains a distant fourth behind PhonePe, Google Pay and Paytm in a market processing more than 20 billion transactions per month.

Industry executives say Shah's appointment signals Meta's ambitions to transform WhatsApp into something closer to a super-app — a single platform for messaging, payments, commerce, lending and financial services. China's WeChat provides the template; India, Brazil and Indonesia offer the addressable market.

"Understanding how people use WhatsApp in markets such as India requires a level of intuition that cannot easily be acquired through research alone," Cox wrote in an internal memo. "It's almost like speaking a language."

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the global Indian community, the appointment carries weight beyond corporate strategy. Shah is the latest in a growing cohort of Indian-origin leaders at the helm of the world's most consequential technology products — joining Sundar Pichai at Alphabet, Satya Nadella at Microsoft, and Arvind Krishna at IBM. But unlike his peers, Shah did not rise through a Western corporate ladder. He built companies in India, for Indian consumers, and was recruited on the strength of that experience.

He will operate from Bengaluru rather than Silicon Valley, underscoring a shift in where global technology decisions are increasingly being made.

For the millions of NRIs who rely on WhatsApp as their primary link to family, community and commerce across borders, the question now is whether Shah can close the gap between what WhatsApp is and what it could become — a platform that does not just carry messages but moves money, sells goods and serves as the operating system for everyday life in the world's fastest-growing digital economies.

nri_angle: An Indian entrepreneur who built his companies in India — not through a Western corporate ladder — now runs the messaging app that millions of NRIs rely on daily to stay connected with family and community.
